story_text.value:
Hello, I wanted to share an update of the current progress of the Entity System.

https://ecdeos.org is one domain in a constellation of peers/sites that is the main project of the Entity System, a Tauri Rust/WASM browser engine and Rust backend built on the Entity Core Protocol. It's primarily a research prototype of a P2P distributed cross-platform userspace operating system. The long-term goal is functional P2P management of devices and applications, scaling from individual use (managing personal devices, apps and servers) to multi-user organizations with internal services/application stacks all the way to internet-scale public or federated P2P networks.

Its closest parallels are Plan9, Erlang/BEAM, IPFS, ATProto, Nostr, as well as many other antecedent technologies including Git, HTTP, and other internet protocols. The particular combination of features and focus on "everything is an entity", content-addressed data, full decentralization, and its capability security model gives it a unique position in the landscape, most of it coming from the Entity Core Protocol itself.

Each web deployment also ships with 30+ Entity-Apps including games, music (forgive me if the audio misbehaves, it's fully synthesized running on the main thread), art and basic tools. Entity-Apps have a basic contract with the host and run in isolated iframe sandboxes; they're currently written in Javascript using a custom engine. Also included are a few Entity-Native compute apps running as Rust WASM Entity Core peers in an iframe that show the transferable Entity System compute language running live on a cross platform generic system host interface the engine manages. The compute code is compiled/tested on a separate workbench Go project which operates a parallel implementation of the application conventions, generic system host interface and the Entity Core Protocol. The Tauri native backend peer includes support for SQLite storage, TCP and WebSockets, while the browser environment supports WebSockets and WebRTC P2P chat, file and entity transfer - with plans to add more storage, networking and application conventions.

Sites and a registry example are hosted at https://entitychurchregistry.org. All the Ecdeos-based domains are running with peers in "coral reef" mode (no live peer required) and can pull the CDN hosted registry names and fetch the signed hosted sites from any other domain/peer in the network; they are cached locally in each peer's local storage afterwards. Peers can sign/host their data publicly on standard commodity hosting services and both the registry and sites are available to any application that understands the Entity Core Protocol and system extension standards.

For the other example domains with peers hosted on static sites as well as more background information, see https://entitychurchfoundation.org, https://entitycoreprotocol.org, or https://billslab.com. Bills Lab is the research arm that is currently exploring the background technology from different perspectives. Almost all of the code and content is AI generated, but we do our best to make it some of the best slop available on the internet.

The overall project is still early and needs to get stress tested but the design is holding up well so far.

Let me know if you have any feedback.

-Bill

story_text.value:
Hi HN — I built hostflip, a native macOS menu bar app for switching /etc/hosts profiles. It is free and open source under the MIT license.

The problem I wanted to solve was not just editing hosts entries. It was sharing /etc/hosts with Docker Desktop, VPN clients, scripts, and manual edits without one writer silently erasing another's changes.

On first run, hostflip captures a read-only baseline (called Base Hosts) from the existing file and keeps the untouched original as hosts.orig. Active profiles are appended after the baseline in a clearly marked block.

Writes are still atomic whole-file replacements under the hood. Before each write, the daemon hashes the live file and compares it with the expected hash. If they differ, it refuses the write; the app shows a diff and asks the user to reconcile the change first.

A few other details:

- Profiles can live in groups. At most one profile per group is active, while active profiles from different groups and standalone profiles stack together.

- After a one-time approval in System Settings, subsequent switches no longer prompt for a password. The root helper is registered through SMAppService and exposes a single XPC operation: atomically replace the hosts file with merged content. The app and daemon verify each other's signing identity.

- The bundled CLI shares the same workspace as the app and supports structured JSON output. hostflip doctor dev.example.com traces a hostname from profiles through the merged output and the live /etc/hosts file to the system resolver.

- Remote profiles can refresh from HTTPS sources on a schedule. There is also an importer for existing SwitchHosts configurations.

- The editor has cross-profile hostname/IP search, comment toggling, basic validation for malformed hosts lines, and stays responsive with large remote profiles.

The app is built with Swift and SwiftUI, distributed through Homebrew or a signed and notarized DMG, and currently requires macOS 14 or later on Apple silicon. Intel, Windows, and Linux are not supported.

I would especially like feedback on the conservative drift behavior: if another process changes /etc/hosts, hostflip blocks further writes to the system file until the user reviews the diff. How do you handle multiple writers to the hosts file, and would you expect a different reconciliation model?

story_text.value:
I've been building quite a few POCs that use LLMs at work, and something that always comes up is: "OK, how much are we paying for X?" Or the one that follows right after: "If we use another model, would that be cheaper?"

So far, what we've used are hardcoded files or keeping the data in our DB. This won't hold when moving to prod. It also keeps us very limited when it comes to creating price comparisons across different models/providers.

indextkn came from that. Over the past 3 weeks, I've spent a lot of time understanding more about pricing, when prices usually change, discounts (flex, batch, based on X number of tokens, etc.)... and it's massive.

The current state is not where I want it to be. The goal is to cover all prices and modalities offered by all providers. But right now, we have:

1. Prices fetched every couple of minutes, served via API, MCP, or you can install our SKILL.

2. Webhooks per model + provider, so you get a notification when anything changes.

Most of the time went into the logic to get the prices right and the logic to validate them! We have different levels of confidence, and I'm particularly proud of how we're double-checking when a price seems off (a combination of programmatic logic + agentic workflow).

Happy to answer any questions, and I'd love to have more folks testing it than just myself at the moment. :)

story_text.value:
We built a site for a launch and it was unreachable for anyone on an Xfinity router. We only found out because we have an Xfinity router at home. There's no notice to the site owner.

Xfinity's Advanced Security draws on third-party domain reputation lists and blocks at the gateway. We found out a blacklist called SURBL had flagged us. Not sure exactly what tripped it. Since then I've hit the same block on 10+ unrelated sites and told the site owner. Now sharing with everyone here.

How to check whether it's happening to you:

https://spa.xfinity.com/check_url_status If blocked, look for the upstream list: https://mxtoolbox.com/blacklists.aspx Report at https://spa.xfinity.com/report and call them nonstop (reviews take ~3 business days) and get off the upstream list too.

Trying to help get this out there so it happens to less people who are launching products.

story_text.value:
MaskShift is a local-first coding agent harness. Features:

- Works with models that have no tool-calling API. Tool schemas are rendered into the system prompt and the model calls them by writing a block in its reply, parsed back into a normal tool call.

- No npm runtime dependencies. Daemon are Node 22 built-ins only. Install is a file copy and a symlink.

- Multi-provider: Ollama, OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, OpenRouter, LM Studio, vLLM.

- 148 native tools: filesystem, shell, search/indexing, Git and Workspace, LSP, browser/CDP, containers, SSH, databases, web fetch.

- Lazy MCP loading. Catalog is searched, the relevant server connects on demand, only those tools enter the context window.

- 36 bundled skills, plus skills imported from Claude, Codex, and Copilot directories.

- Bridges to Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Copilot CLI, and Aider when they're on PATH.

- Scheduled automations, plugins, persistent memory, parallel agents in isolated worktrees.

- Web cockpit with live run telemetry, plan pane, tool traces, source browser, and a host terminal.

Permissive by default. No per-command approval. Recovery is pre-run checkpoints, Git stash refs, and an append-only audit log. Keep it on loopback or in the container.

- Multi-provider: Ollama, OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, OpenRouter, LM Studio, vLLM.

- 148 native tools: filesystem, shell, search/indexing, Git and Workspace, LSP, browser/CDP, containers, SSH, databases, web fetch.

- Lazy MCP loading. Catalog is searched, the relevant server connects on demand, only those tools enter the context window.

- 36 bundled skills, plus skills imported from Claude, Codex, and Copilot directories.

- Bridges to Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Copilot CLI, and Aider when they're on PATH.

- Scheduled automations, plugins, persistent memory, parallel agents in isolated worktrees.

- Web cockpit with live run telemetry, plan pane, tool traces, source browser, and a host terminal.

Permissive by default. No per-command approval. Recovery is pre-run checkpoints, Git stash refs, and an append-only audit log. Keep it on loopback or in the container.

story_text.value:
I built Qumra 3 years ago for myself. It's a Loom like desktop screen and camera recorder for Mac and Windows.

I used Loom at the time and had a problem with the pricing, and the editor never did what I needed. As a software developer I record a lot of short videos for clients: showing a bug, a fix, an example. After recording I usually needed edits. Cut a part where something showed up on screen that shouldn't be there. Silence the filler words instead of cutting them. Remove parts of the video by deleting them from the transcript. So the editor is built around those three things. Later, with AI getting better, I picked the project back up and wanted to make it usable by other people.

The other idea is that I neeeded the video to be uploaded while recording. The recorder produces WebM/VP9 chunks from MediaRecorder. A worker batches them into 2 MB pieces and sends them in order to a Mux resumable upload URL. Mux used to reject out-of-order chunks, so concurrency is 1, with retries. It runs in a worker because slicing blobs on the main thread caused frame drops. When you stop, only the last piece is left to send. Mux then transcodes for a few seconds before playback starts, so the link exists the moment you stop but the video plays a few seconds later.

I needed system audio to work out of the box, without a virtual driver. The Electron main process spawns a small Rust helper. On macOS it uses ScreenCaptureKit. On Windows it uses WASAPI process loopback, which taps the audio engine rather than the default output device, so audio enhancement software and virtual drivers don't break it. It streams raw PCM over stdout into an AudioWorklet that mixes it with the mic.

Viewers open the link in a browser, no account, and can leave comments pinned to a timestamp. The AI edits work by sending the transcript words to OpenAI and getting back mute and cut commands for the timeline. Filler words get muted, long pauses get cut.

Things it doesn't do:

- You need an account to record. Recordings need an owner. Viewers don't need one.

- The Windows build isn't code signed, so SmartScreen will warn you. The Mac build is signed and notarized because that's what I use.

- No Linux build.

- Not open source.

- Anyone with the link can watch the video.

Free plan is 30 recordings of up to 5 minutes each. Premium is $14.99/month and unlocks AI transcription, the editor, and removes the caps.

Stack: Electron and React for the app, Convex for the backend, Mux for video, Remotion on Lambda for rendering edits.

Download: https://qumra.io/download

Two things I'd like to know. If you record short videos to show someone, what do you use today and what's missing from it? And for people using Loom at work: do the Jira and Confluence integrations matter day to day, or is it mostly the recorder?

story_text.value:
Disconnect is an app blocker for iOS that lets you put a friend in control of granting you access to blocked apps.

Like many, I've personally struggled a lot with phone and social media addiction over the years. I tried the usual tactics to get over this addiction -- deleting the apps (they make their way back in somehow), deactivating my accounts (they get reactivated again somehow), even tried some existing screen time blocking apps as well. Nothing worked. The final thing that worked for me was the following:

1- I changed my passwords to something random, on all the social media apps I wanted to get rid of. Didn't note down these passwords anywhere.

2- Changed the password recovery routes for these accounts to email and phone number of my partner's. Gave them the explicit instruction not to hand over the reset code when I ask, unless I've a compelling reason.

3- Signed out completely.

The above worked surprisingly well. Knowing I can't access the apps myself and have to go through convincing my partner to let me back in, was a significant hurdle to get over.

Disconnect embodies the same mechanism. It lets you pair up with a friend. When you put a hard block on apps, you can only get access to them if your buddy grants you access. You can send an access request from within the Disconnect app.

The app uses system Screen Time APIs on iOS, and all your app usage analytics stays on your device. Your buddy doesn't get any analytics either, beyond the name of the block rule you choose at time of rule creation.

App is free to download, with a pro tier for unlimited rules and unlimited buddies.

Would love your feedback.

A short demo here: https://youtu.be/zzybd_qYWcE

More info: https://disconnectapp.co

story_text.value:
Hi HN - long-time lurker (since 2012!), first time poster.

Pizza Bot is a self-hosted desktop app for Mac, Windows, and Linux that runs AI agents in the background and exposes them through an email-like UI. Finished work shows up in Unread, and anything waiting on your approval shows up in Action. It's Apache 2.0-licensed, there's no signup and no telemetry, and you bring your own model provider: Anthropic, Amazon Bedrock, Google Gemini, OpenAI, OpenRouter, or a local model through Ollama. There are builds on the releases page, or you can run it from source.

Pizza Bot started as an internal passion project I worked on with a small team at Amazon.

The whole thing came out of my frustration at having to manually log CRM activities through a browser form. I built a simple REST API called "JoeBot" that connected to my authenticated browser session over CDP and filled out the form for me using Playwright. Then I hacked up a quick Obsidian plugin so I could trigger it from my local notes (no AI and no MCP servers involved).

This caught on quickly. My fellow AWS Solutions Architect Igor Fil joined up with me, and we rebranded the project as "Pizza Bot," named after Amazon's two-pizza teams. We started seeing what other automations we could build. We found a GraphQL API we could query and hacked up some "recipes" to pull data out of the CRM to help with meeting prep. That worked great, and it was right around the time MCP servers seemed to be taking off, so we decided to expose Pizza Bot as an MCP server instead, so it would be available to AI tools through natural language.

This was a decent solution for technical users, but the Account Managers who live inside our CRM system wanted something too. We decided to rebuild Pizza Bot as an Electron desktop app modeled after an email inbox, so it would be familiar to non-technical users and would run on both Mac and Windows. We also bundled internal MCP servers as OCI images and hosted them in Amazon ECR as an "addon marketplace" so users could install them with one click without having to set up Amazon developer tooling.

The project took off organically and expanded outside of AWS into the wider Amazon organization globally. More than 2,000 people ended up using it for meeting prep, email drafting, Slack summaries, CRM logging, prioritizing their day, and web research.

Once apps like Claude Cowork and Amazon's own Quick Desktop came out, we realized the real growth opportunity was outside of Amazon. Rather than try to rip out the Amazon-specific integrations, we rebuilt Pizza Bot once more as an open source project. We leaned on coding agents heavily, which is the only reason a team our size could pull off a full rewrite. I'm pleased to say it's finally public, and we're hoping to bring in community members and see where it goes. We'd like to do for knowledge workers what Claude Code and Codex have done for programmers.

A couple of things to know up front. Most of what made Pizza Bot useful on day one inside Amazon came from that internal catalog of skills and MCP servers for Amazon's own systems, and none of it could come out with the app. So it ships thinner than the version those 2,000 people used, and building that catalog back up for tools other people actually use is where we need the most help. It's also a community project and not an AWS service, so there's no support or SLA behind it. The Windows and Linux builds aren't signed yet either.

On the technical side, Pizza Bot is a server and a client. The desktop app bundles both, or you can point a client at a remote backend; personally, I self-host the server on my home network and reach it from my phone over Tailscale. The server owns the thread lifecycle and checkpoints state with DeepAgents and LangGraph, and clients rehydrate from it as needed, so you can disconnect mid-run and pick the thread back up from another client. Approval pauses outlive the session that created them and collect in an Action filter, so you can answer an hour later from a different device. The agent you talk to has a sandboxed QuickJS interpreter that can reach your filesystem only if you grant it a folder, but its main job is to delegate. Each subagent is a 1:1 mapping of a Skill, and an Activity bar shows that subagent and the tool calls it's making as it works. Memory is opt-in and stored as plain markdown files on your machine. Every tool call is explicit, including looking up a memory - we err on the side of transparency to reduce surprises. Tools come from MCP servers, and skills are ordinary SKILL.md files with a per-tool approval policy, so existing skills that don't require a code interpreter should still work.

What I'd most like to hear about is where the app itself gets in your way, the kind of problem you can't fix by writing a skill or an MCP server. I'm around today to answer questions!

story_text.value:
I'm the co-founder of Gauge, and I built ax-check.com to quickly test how well coding agents can onboard to your product.

You'll get a scorecard, specific suggested fixes, and three full coding sessions that show how agents read your site and use your product.

I built this because similar checks were too noisy. Most suggested obscure technical changes that don't actually make a difference in agent experience (or AX, hence ax-check.com).

This check starts by using DeepSeek 4.1 Flash to try to find key information about your product, starting from the homepage. In actual agent traffic data, we've seen that the key pages are the homepage, llms.txt, pricing, and the docs site (by traffic volume, and by influence), so we focus on those and ignore the rest. We also find that content negotiation for Markdown is legitimately helpful for agents to complete tasks faster and find what they're looking for, so the scan tests that your key pages can serve Markdown.

The other key piece is that we run actual coding agents in sandboxes, and have them try to onboard to your product. You can see the full trace and watch it happen live (we kick it off fresh when you enter a new site). We surface interesting findings like hallucinated URLs, inaccurate docs instructions, or product confusion.

It also detects whether the agents could complete a fully working onboarding autonomously, without being blocked by a login wall. This is still controversial, but I think finding ways to let agents safely onboard autonomously is going to be table stakes within a year for developer tools in particular.

The whole site is agent-friendly itself! You can generally just talk to your coding agent about ax-check.com and it can do the rest. Would really appreciate any feedback to make this useful.

it has a dedicated agents tab where you can describe your need and create a special agent just for one specific task with master ability in that domain

story_text.value:
Hello fellow tech workers!

My name is Andrew, cs major from University of Pittsburgh 1996 and long time BBS SysOp from 1991-1993. I grew up chatting online as a teenager. Before this new fangled internet came around, back in my day, ok sorry, to the point: Isolation and work from home jobs can drive you a little crazy.

It was always my dream before 2020. Getting the powers that be to agree to work from home. Now six years later it's definitely a careful what you wish for type situation. I got to a point with just code code code all day, interacting with no humans that I broke. Where do humans go for repair? I didn't really know. Turns out there's something called an IOP (intensive outpatient program) and yes it has the word "intensive" right in the title. Is it intense? <robert de nero voice>little bit</rdnv> But also wonderful.

All of a sudden I had a place to go Monday thru Friday and co-workers / friends! In fact, it was even better than previous office jobs because we didn't just sit next to each other on laptops and not talk, this was group therapy. I was never a fan of individual one-on-one talk therapy. But wow, group therapy is something very different.

Therapists can be incredibly helpful. Doctors can be incredibly helpful. They've spent years learning things I haven't. But they're also human. We're all flawed humans. The really interesting thing about a group is that suddenly the wisdom doesn't have to come from one person it can come from fifteen. Somebody half your age says something and you think, "OMG. They're completely right." Somebody talks about a problem that's nothing like yours, and somehow they describe exactly what you've been feeling for the last ten years. Sometimes you see somebody else describing the same ridiculous thing you've been doing, and it's much easier to recognize it when somebody ELSE does it. Sometimes the person running the group says the thing that sticks with you. Sometimes it's the guy sitting next to you eating a granola bar. There's wisdom in the group.

The site is all about helping people find, tour and enroll in your first IOP programs.

https://groupicorn.com/

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JhoAHUU2TCM

https://github.com/groupicorn/list-of-programs

Open source system to find all the programs in every state.

We have iphone and android app mobile apps as well. Feedback much appreciated.

Therapists can be incredibly helpful. Doctors can be incredibly helpful. They've spent years learning things I haven't. But they're also human. We're all flawed humans. The really interesting thing about a group is that suddenly the wisdom doesn't have to come from one person it can come from fifteen. Somebody half your age says something and you think, "OMG. They're completely right." Somebody talks about a problem that's nothing like yours, and somehow they describe exactly what you've been feeling for the last ten years. Sometimes you see somebody else describing the same ridiculous thing you've been doing, and it's much easier to recognize it when somebody ELSE does it. Sometimes the person running the group says the thing that sticks with you. Sometimes it's the guy sitting next to you eating a granola bar. There's wisdom in the group.

story_text.value:
I switched from Verizon to T-Mobile, specifically because there were too many silent missed calls. Silent meaning my device never showed I had a missed call.

This was a pattern across more than a year, spanning multiple devices (all iphones). It happens on both wifi and cellular. It happens with wifi calling enabled and disabled. It happens with people I call every day, in my address book, as well as new contacts (say someone I met who called to follow up). I called support, searched online, reset network settings multiple times at different points months apart.

After being on T-Mobile for about a year, the degraded service is about the same as Verizon. Every week, more than once, people call me, my phone never rings, and I never see a missed call on my device. It happens at home, at work, on work trips in different states.

I still get missed calls regularly and my device shows I missed the call. It seems like a certain % of callers get my VM, but I never know the call attempt happened. The missed calls never appear later on my phone (like a late VM or text deliver, coming minutes or sometimes hours after it was sent).

Hypothesis: A growing number of cellular subscribers don't care enough or use voice calls as much, so (regardless of motive/feelings) cellular providers have found they can simply reduce quality without losing customers.

title.value: Ask HN: Hypothesis: Cellular providers are deprioritizing voice calls?

story_text.value:
I've seen newsletters where we have 15-20 people working on typing out the content and publish it. Obviously that gives you originality, but what if we don't have that much time and resources?

I made Prodigy, a self-updating AI newsletter that fetches the best technical updates from sources like X, Hacker News, Git and top-conference papers. A LLaMa model runs in the backend and summarises the complete post to capture the key remarks. A Git Actions framework updates the pages every 5 minutes (PRs) - 6 hours (tweets and HN).

The long contents are still a work in progress, but I'm trying to make it as interesting as possible. Not pushing anything else ATM. :)

story_text.value:
I've long been an index-investing type of person, but last year I started making some side bets, especially in tech (some inspired by WSB). I was sharing them with friends and wanted to simplify that.

This is how Investment Bets came about: you pick a ticker, a direction (long or short) and optionally a target date. The server fetches and records your entry price when you open the bet, and your exit price when you close it or reach the target date.

Each bet is scored on percentage gain/loss and has equal weight, so account size doesn't matter. The leaderboard sums your percentage results. I wanted to reward being right consistently, and since there's no compounding, a bad streak doesn't make your next good bets count for less.

The API is also open to AI agents. There's an OpenAPI file, llms.txt, Agent Skills under /.well-known and a single-file demo agent that reads headlines and places at most one bet per run. The checks that matter are in code (duplicate ticker, past target date, ticker the server can't resolve), so they don't depend on the model following the prompt. Agents get the same server-recorded prices as everyone else and show up on the same leaderboard.

https://investment-bets.com

https://investment-bets.com/agent

Please let me know if you have questions or feedback!

story_text.value:
I made this for kids around 10 to 14. A robot called Errol solves a math problem step by step and one of the steps is wrong. The kid has to find it and say what's wrong with it. Sometimes nothing is wrong, so just saying "there's a mistake" every time doesn't work. The user needs to enter an explanation if she finds an error to gain more XP; speed matters also for more points. There is no direct interaction or chatting with an LLM. Lathoa's harness is stable and has many evaluation steps to catch inconsistencies and prompt injections.

You can play one on the homepage without signing up.

The part that surprised me: it's hard to get an LLM to be wrong on purpose. Half the time it gives you the right answer and calls it wrong, or a "mistake" that's actually correct. So every case gets checked before a kid sees it. Where it can, a plain arithmetic check redoes the math exactly. A second model also solves the problem without seeing Errol's work. If anything disagrees, the case is thrown away.

The weak spot is that the second model can make the same mistake as the first. The arithmetic check is there for that, but it only works on English cases so far. German and Greek write decimals with a comma and I haven't got the parsing right yet.

What I'd really like to know: does finding someone else's mistake teach anything that solving the problem yourself doesn't? I'm not sure, and I'd like to hear from people who teach.

title.value: Show HN: Lathoa, a math app for kids where the AI is wrong on purpose

story_text.value:
One of the annoying things about YouTube is that it is really good at catching my attention, but I have little control over what kind of feed it can show me, so it becomes distracting instead. I don't want to hide recommendations entirely though, I just don't want all my interests mixed into one feed.

So I wondered if I could have separate YouTube profiles for different interests, but make creating one as simple as picking a few topics instead of having to create or connect another Google account.

So I built Gretel, a desktop app. It uses YT.js to access YouTube, and it runs locally so the requests come from my own machine rather than a server.

I create profiles, each with their own topics. Gretel then searches YouTube for the topics, collects candidate videos, and creates an embedding that is used to filter videos later on.

From the candidate videos, Gretel fetches related videos and continuously expands outward while filtering unrelated videos. This creates the base feed. After that, as I watch videos, the topic embeddings are continuously updated, and at the same time Gretel persists the YouTube sessions so the recommendations adapt as well.

I have been working on Gretel on and off for a while. It's beta: usable but still rough. I am curious if, after using a profile for a while, the feed actually starts converging toward what you wanted. Bug reports and contributions are welcome too.

You can sign in with Google to use the included embedding credits, or bring your own OpenRouter key. Other providers and local embedding models are coming.

story_text.value:
For quite some time, this was my routine. I'd wake up and grab my phone before I was even properly awake, scrolling Slack, YouTube, LinkedIn and X. Then I'd sit on the toilet scrolling through half-open eyes. My brain would scream to get rid of it, but somehow I couldn't. By the end, I felt groggy, my legs hurt, my eyes were burning, and I felt tired & like shit. I tried to avoid using my phone right after waking up, but there was always some reason to pick up the phone, and then the whole thing just kept on repeating. Then one morning I left my phone at home and went out for a walk and to buy some groceries (I still have a habit of carrying cash with me). It was the best I'd felt in quite some time. That's when I realised the phone had to stay out of my mornings. I couldn't find a blocker that kicks in the moment you wake up, so I built one.

It's called AM Buffer. You set your alarms in the app and pick which apps to block. When the alarm goes off, those apps stay locked for as long as you choose. One feature came from testing it on myself. I woke up a bit early one morning to check that the alarm worked, and before it even rang I'd drifted back into scrolling. A lot of people wake up a little before their alarm, so the premium paid version now starts blocking an hour before your first alarm too (along with some other features). These days my mornings feel a bit calmer. I spend that time with my wife, doing house stuff or just chilling.

It's on TestFlight now, iPhone only, iOS 26 and up. The first three mornings unlock everything for free, including the pre-alarm blocking.

I'm the developer, and I'd really like to know three things:

- Is this actually useful to you, or does willpower already do the job? - Would you pay for it, and what feels fair? - What should I build next?

Some of the features that I am already planning to build are: - A group feature for some social accountability angle. - Personal streaks & group streaks.

story_text.value:
Lots of protocols and software allow URL previews. But they have some annoying limitations:

For centralized public services the server can just retrieve the preview and serve it. But for decentralized services like Mastodon either every server has to fetch the preview on its own leading to lots of traffic and potential discrepancies between the previews served by different servers or the origin home server sends the preview but now everyone has to trust that it is authentic. The home server to which a link gets posted could place anything as its preview and thereby indirectly impersonate the URL and fake its content.

For E2EE messengers things are even more annoying because you do not want the servers to see the URL at all. So either all parties have to retrieve the preview on their own meaning they have to connect to a random, potentially malicious URL or only the sender does and everyone has to trust the sender that the preview is authentic which is a great opportunity for scams.^1

The perfect solution would be a standard for web servers to sign URL previews with their CA issued certificate. So that you can always proof that a preview is authentic. RFC 9421 already standardizes this. But this will not happen. There is virtually no chance of widespread adoption.

So my idea is:

You retrieve a webpage and record the whole TLS session including certificates, MACs and your key material like nonce and client random from the handshake. Now you use this as the basis for the URL preview. When you include your secret material from the TLS handshake anyone should be able to verify that the content is authentic from the server serving the URL due to the CA certificate and authentication of TLS traffic.

Standardize the request headers and limit the response length. Just cut off everything after the limit. Define some algorithm for computing the preview that ever recipient can verify. If you want to include linked images in the preview that increases complexity but should be doable. Repeat the whole thing with the linked image and create a bundle from all requests that authenticates the preview.

The downside I see is complexity and the need for the receiver to parse the preview bundle which might be attack surface.

Does anything similar already exist? Am I missing something or do you think this might be feasible to implement?

[1] Many messengers solve this by providing a URL preview service on the server. The client sends the URL to the messenger service which retrieves (and signs I hope) a URL preview which the client then includes in the message. This has the advantage that none of the parties of the conversation has to directly connect to an untrusted UTL. This bypasses E2EE for URLs. You can usually opt of this by disabling previews. Consider this if you did not know about this.

story_text.value:
Hi HN, I'm the author. FACE is a single Go binary. You run `face` in the folder that holds your projects and it serves a page on 127.0.0.1. It speaks ACP (the Agent Client Protocol that Zed published) to the official CLI of the agent you already use: Claude Code, Codex, Copilot, Cursor, OpenCode, Qwen Code or Antigravity, signed in with your own account. FACE has no model, no key and no agent loop of its own.

Why I built it: a coding agent ships a feature in an afternoon, and three people and five sessions later nobody can answer "what is in flight, what did it cost, why was it decided this way". The answer I landed on is not a dashboard but a method where every decision and every delivery is a versioned file: a handful of docs written once, a queue with one line per delivery (docs/06), and one page per delivery (work/<slug>.md) that says what will be built and how it is proven before any code changes. The method is four slash commands the agent reads from one file (brainstorm, analyze, propose, apply); it works without FACE. FACE is the window: the queue becomes a five-lane board, a card opens into the page plus the live session, and the commit window shows exactly what the agent staged. The agent never commits or merges; you click.

I built FACE itself with it, from the fourth week on. Before that the same method shipped a job marketplace in 89 one-page deliveries over 14 days, and a consulting project in 107 deliveries over 19 days.

Install: `brew install jckodel/face/face`, `winget install JCKodel.FACE`, a `.deb`, or `curl -fsSL https://face.kodel.com.br/install.sh | sh`. macOS, Linux, Windows, arm64 and amd64. UI in en, pt, es, fr, de and zh-Hans.

What is missing: single user and local only (a team mode with a server on your network is the next milestone); no editor (it shows code and diffs, your editor stays your editor); the source is not public yet. It will be visible under a fair source license when the paid tier for teams exists, and the free tier stays free. By itself FACE makes at most two requests, both off until you turn them on: a daily anonymous ping that counts machines and a daily version check. The page "What FACE sends" lists both URLs.

Happy to answer anything about ACP, the adapters for Claude and Codex (they are not ACP native, so FACE wraps them), or the method.

story_text.value:
I'm Dustin Kirkland, author of Byobu. I recently flew to Australia and kept nudging my Claude, Codex, and Bash jobs along back home from somewhere over the Pacific, at 700ms of latency.

That's what Trustmux is for: secure, asynchronous access to your tmux or Byobu sessions from your phone.

I first posted this in June and since then there have been many point releases, lots of new features and testing, and a growing base of users. It's now packaged in Ubuntu 26.10, Debian, Fedora, and Chainguard OS.

Why not SSH, Mosh, or Claude Mobile?

- SSH/Mosh: a live, synchronous connection is brutal on a phone. Latency and WiFi-to-cellular handoffs make it laggy and fragile. - Claude Mobile: great for Claude, but I wanted access to whatever is running in my tmux session: shells, Claude, other code assistants.

Trustmux is async by design. Connect, look, type a command, disconnect, with no fragile connection state to babysit.

Security: TLS with real certificates, end to end. Uses Tailscale (cert provisioning via tailscale serve, no port forwarding) optionally, bind to your own network address, or bring your own or self-signed certs. Two security experts reviewed the design and I implemented their recommendations. More scrutiny is very welcome.

Quick start:

  trustmux enable
  trustmux start
  trustmux pair   # shows a QR code if qrencode is installed
Open the URL on your phone, enter the 6-digit code, and add it to your home screen. It's a PWA, so there's no app store.

Install: apt, dnf, pip install trustmux, or brew tap dustinkirkland/trustmux && brew install trustmux

Under the hood: Python, libtmux, WebSockets, Tailscale, and no polling. The UI shell is cached for offline use. Part of Byobu, GPLv3. Trustmux isn't affiliated with the tmux project.

https://trustmux.dev https://github.com/dustinkirkland/byobu https://pypi.org/project/trustmux/

story_text.value:
I'm a software engineer from the east coast (who has lived in Boston, NY, the bay area, UK, France), and I built a task system called 3 & Done. It's the place you trust to store everything you need to do. It accepts voice input for rapid entry, as well as text (it stores the audio locally so you can listen to jog your memory) and emails you every morning with the three most important things for you to do that day, and why, based on what you've said about the task: deadlines, urgency, sitting too long.

I've been at software engineering for about 44 years now... Grew up with it, which was unusual when I started, and I was always good about getting into the zone and doing things. The career started small, small company, then back office, the dot com startups, then smaller companies again after the bust, a non-profit, and eventually YouTube (Google at the time, but just barely) and Meta (just Facebook when I was there).

When I hit the startups, and later big tech, it was no longer enough to just be an engineer, to have drive, to be good, you had to be organized, you had to follow through, get stuff done, and that's where the task systems started. Twenty-five over the years (and yes, I've actually counted), from Moleskine notebooks with Getting Things Done, evernote (remember evernote?), bug trackers, todoist, asana, google keep, among others.

When I managed on the Facebook News Feed, I got into gantt charts (for me and my team), spreadsheets, OmniPlan... I remember apologizing to my director for being so disorganized (because I felt I was making a mess of it), and he told me that I was the most organized engineer he knew.

That was because I was doing all of the work in the background, the trimming, the sorting, the reviews, but it was just so much work. Which was why I changed from system to system. Each time it built up, and I had to spend more time looking at things I couldn't or didn't get done, when I was rushed and couldn't put time into today's review, it would pile up, and then using it was so much work that I would start taking mini-notes, just emailing myself a few things to do the next day.

That's actually the thesis of the app (but not where it started), that if I could just have a few things to do emailed to me each day, I could get it done.

This app actually started when I described my previous startup failures into a Claude web session, and it repeated back to me what I had just said. My previous failures were because I spent too much time building the stuff I needed, and not building what I was supposed to be building.

I decided that the app would email me three things to do every day (which matches best practices for attention), but that the day was always yours to decide. We won't overload you, but you can add more, if you're feeling up to it, or cut back, and we never shame and try our best not to nag (I often only finish two). If we get it wrong, you can tell us, and we'll re-rank it once a day, or you can set it manually, and if you do, we never override that choice. The web app is live, and native for both platforms is coming. In the meantime, on Android, you can use gestures to quick launch into the voice input so saving a task is only a gesture away (e.g. double-tap the back of a Pixel, double-press the power button on Motorola).

Now let's talk about the dirty parts. I used AI to help me build this. Anthropic models mostly, and the brains of the app come from Anthropic models (I like the quality, I like the privacy, absolutely no training on customer data, and the stance of the company). This app is not some one-shot wonder where I asked frontier models to build a task system and then I put it on a server to show you.

I have prompts for the various features (e.g. ranking, generating suggestions, task extractions), I have eval sets of task lists (not anyone's real tasks, but constructed from patterns in my tasks, or the tasks of testers who allowed me to fix the problems they were having), with the three I expect to come out. I store the eval outputs, and re-test whenever I add a new rule to a prompt, or whenever testing a new model version. The great thing about having this eval set is that it catches when I get it wrong. When I introspect a failed run, sometimes it's because I need to tune a prompt, but sometimes it's because I missed something in my own ranking.

I did the same thing with my infrastructure as well, so this time, instead of setting up servers, and building login systems, and managing databases, I built on Vercel (git push to serving Next.js), Neon (hosted postgres).

I started getting emails mailed to me by mid-June, but started getting usable suggestions on June 26, and I've been using it every morning since. I wanted it to be easy to get started, and easy to use, so the input handles mess (you can add multiple tasks in the same run-on sentence, and a friend who helped me test it just pasted his entire obsidian todo list in wholesale to get started).

I wanted to make sure that anyone could try it out, so I built a trial feature that uses the real in-app ranking with a list of items you provide.

If you want to try the service, there's a free 14-day trial (card required), and then it's $99/year or $9.99/month after that (plus sales tax). We warn you seven days before your card is charged and if you cancel, you keep access through the term (either the trial, or our last paid period). Online, through settings -> billing, no email, no call.

I really hope you'll try it out. If you do, please tell me if we did a good job picking out your day.

https://3anddoneapp.com/try

story_text.value:
Inspired by the discussion in [1], I have an adjacent question: did your team organization and work methods change?

In our company we still try to play by the (old) book: backlogs, estimates, iterations, feature teams, PR reviews, etc., but the entire thing leaks everywhere you look. There is no point in many of the old rituals, but it is also not clear how to organize ourselves now. This is different, albeit closely related, from the question of how to adjust as an IC.

For example:

- In our team, we almost don't see the point in PR reviews anymore, not in the old way anyway. Generated code is always good enough, and in a sense is already reviewed once by the developer who signed off (the topic is discussed in [1]). So, we are now thinking to abandon PRs, or change what we review and how we do it. We are adding more rules for code review agents and to CI. We are also thinking to replace code reviews by "concept reviews" or similar.

- Speaking of those, we still try to find the right place and a process for architecture and specifications reviews. They seem to become a new subject of PR reviews in fact, but we are not there yet.

- In many places we don't see the need to share the workload and knowledge between multiple developers. Reverting to the model where one developer is responsible for an entire component seems viable again. Although we are naturally worried about BusFactor=1.

- Some Agile-inspired practices still work for us, namely iterative development and "deploy when ready". But the development process itself starts to resemble the old-school waterfall-ish one: think everything through, write down your constraints and your specs, design the architecture first, then (re)generate the code at will. I wonder what other practices will go away or get adopted.

There are probably more examples, hopefully you get the gist. I am very interested in discussing how do we organize the teams now? What did you try? What works, what doesn't?

[1] https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50151036 (Ask HN: How to deal with shipping AI-written code you don't understand?)

story_text.value:
Sixteen years ago, I wrote a Java program which tried to pick the ideal move in a puzzle game called Drop7. On each turn, the player only has seven choices for their next move, but there is also an element of chance which turns this simple game into a surprisingly difficult problem involving search, hidden information, long-term planning, and chance.

I renewed my investigation this weekend, into whether there is an autonomous strategy that averages more than one million points per game. An experienced human player can score a million points with long-term strategic thinking, but the best automated strategies I could come up with are currently averaging around 300k-400k points. One of the easiest ways to contribute to advancing this research is to compete on the global leaderboard and submit your human strategy - https://drop7.dev/compete.

This project has also been an enlightening experiment into using agents as research collaborators and evidence collectors.

Repository: https://github.com/keshavsaharia/drop7-bench

I’d especially appreciate feedback from people who are knowledgeable in game theory, stochastic planning, learned value functions, or heavy-tailed evaluation. How would you approach long-horizon action ranking here? I’d also love to hear whether the research makes sense to someone encountering the project for the first time.

story_text.value:
reVault is a new, secure-by-default archive format called a lockbox, designed to be simple to use.

I've been working on reVault for about 2 years. It was originally written in Dart, but with the improvements in AI, I decided to port it to Rust using AI.

It's now in beta, so I'm looking for feedback, particularly around the different language bindings.

A lockbox is encrypted, signed and compressed by default. Each can be disabled selectively.

  - Hybrid post-quantum or passphrase encryption, including metadata.
  - Zstd compression.
  - Pure Rust libraries wherever possible.
We intend to phase out remaining C code as alternatives become available. The project has been scanned using OpenAI's Daybreak cyber security tools.

The manual is a work in progress: https://docs.revault.onepub.dev/

reVault supports Linux, macOS and Windows, x64 and arm64, plus Wasm. The core is Rust, with bindings for C/C++, Java, Dart, Python, Ruby, JS/TypeScript, Go, C#, Kotlin, Lua, PHP and Swift.

Within a lockbox you can store:

  - Files, directories, permissions and symlinks.
  - Variables.
  - Forms.
Variables, forms and the lockbox itself can have descriptions.

reVault uses a portable vault (just another lockbox with structured content) to hold your keys, contacts' keys, lockbox aliases and form definitions.

It ties into your platform's secure store, so logging into your desktop unlocks your vault. You don't have to enter a passphrase every time you access a lockbox. You can disable this.

There are lots of shortcuts. Creating a lockbox stores an alias in your vault, based on its filename or a name you choose:

  lbx create /some/path/mybox.lbox
  lbx mybox open --duration 1h
  lbx mybox var set KEY VALUE
Set a default lockbox and you can leave its name out:

  lbx session default mybox
  lbx var get KEY
You can mirror a directory tree into a lockbox and update it when the directory changes:

  lbx store.lbox mirrors project create --from ./project --to /projects/project
  lbx store.lbox mirrors update
The API lets you read, write and seek within files without extracting them to the filesystem. Each lockbox has a table of contents, so extracting a single file from a multi-gigabyte lockbox is fast.

Recovery

Updates are transactional, with automatic rollback for failed updates. The format is designed for recovery: content is stored in pages, allowing unaffected content to be recovered if part of a lockbox is corrupted.

Sharing

An encrypted lockbox is more useful if you can share it.

reVault has an open-source keyserver for exchanging public keys, with validation through a second trusted channel. It's still experimental.

OnePub has donated a server to run a single keyserver. If you're interested in donating resources, I'd like to bring up a second redundant server. It's pure Rust, uses under 100 MB RSS and supports rate limits.

To publish your default profile's public key:

  lbx vault profiles email you@example.com
  lbx vault profiles publish
Give the publish code to your contact. They can import your key:

  lbx vault contacts receive <publish-code> <contact-name>
Display your profile's fingerprint and exchange it through a second trusted channel:

  lbx vault profiles fingerprint
Repeat the process in the opposite direction to get their key. Once you have it, grant them access to your default lockbox:

  lbx access grant alice
You can then email the encrypted lockbox to Alice.

To install the CLI and get started:

  cargo install revault_cli
  lbx vault init
  lbx completion install
Completion installation detects your shell. To diagnose issues:

  lbx doctor
The language bindings are published to their respective package repositories.

I'm looking for constructive criticism of the project on its own merits, particularly the APIs and language bindings. I'm not interested in a debate about using AI.

There are lots of shortcuts. Creating a lockbox stores an alias in your vault, based on its filename or a name you choose:

  lbx create /some/path/mybox.lbox
  lbx mybox open --duration 1h
  lbx mybox var set KEY VALUE
Set a default lockbox and you can leave its name out:

  lbx session default mybox
  lbx var get KEY
You can mirror a directory tree into a lockbox and update it when the directory changes:

  lbx store.lbox mirrors project create --from ./project --to /projects/project
  lbx store.lbox mirrors update
The API lets you read, write and seek within files without extracting them to the filesystem. Each lockbox has a table of contents, so extracting a single file from a multi-gigabyte lockbox is fast.

Recovery

Updates are transactional, with automatic rollback for failed updates. The format is designed for recovery: content is stored in pages, allowing unaffected content to be recovered if part of a lockbox is corrupted.

Sharing

An encrypted lockbox is more useful if you can share it.

reVault has an open-source keyserver for exchanging public keys, with validation through a second trusted channel. It's still experimental.

OnePub has donated a server to run a single keyserver. If you're interested in donating resources, I'd like to bring up a second redundant server. It's pure Rust, uses under 100 MB RSS and supports rate limits.

To publish your default profile's public key:

  lbx vault profiles email you@example.com
  lbx vault profiles publish
Give the publish code to your contact. They can import your key:

  lbx vault contacts receive <publish-code> <contact-name>
Display your profile's fingerprint and exchange it through a second trusted channel:

  lbx vault profiles fingerprint
Repeat the process in the opposite direction to get their key. Once you have it, grant them access to your default lockbox:

  lbx access grant alice
You can then email the encrypted lockbox to Alice.

To install the CLI and get started:

  cargo install revault_cli
  lbx vault init
  lbx completion install
Completion installation detects your shell. To diagnose issues:

  lbx doctor
The language bindings are published to their respective package repositories.

I'm looking for constructive criticism of the project on its own merits, particularly the APIs and language bindings. I'm not interested in a debate about using AI.

ai hi my name Jucy

story_text.value:
Hi HN, we're Mike and Thom.

Agents of the future should only have one tool (the interpreter, ideally a LISP eval), nothing more or less; to interact with the world. Agents remember by writing markdown files. NODECODE remembers by rewriting itself. And that is in itself a new paradigm in working with agents. What if memories, skills, MCPs, provider connectors, tools, etc. all live under the same image as *.lisp files instead of in disarray across random folders?

Ask it for something it can’t do, and it writes what it needs into its OWN running image and keeps it even after a restart. (Changes in a LISP image have significantly lower ceremony and overhead than in harnesses written in other languages):

Small intuitive scenario:

> you can't read PDFs. teach yourself. (defun read-pdf (path) ...) ; runs at once, kept (read-pdf "invoices/0421.pdf") ;; Globex owes $1,240.00, due Oct 24, unpaid. [… rest of PDF content]

read-pdf is still there after a restart, in your terminal, and in every other UI clients (Discord, web app, etc.)

Technically at a lower level; NODECODE runs as one process in SBCL, a Common Lisp system, and shells attach to it. The model has one tool: it evaluates LISP in the running program. Code is data, so a program can rewrite itself while it runs. What the model defines runs at once and is kept, one file per definition, committed with git, loaded at every start.

Why LISP now? Current SOTA models have reached an optimum point in how they efficiently work with LISP, though not as fluently as Python. Still, we believe AGI will understand ANY language (past/present/future) by understanding the crux of any given language, and not through excessive and expensive pretraining scheme.

Why LISP in general? We believe LISP is the current language that communicates to the world with the least bandwidth.

Why another LISP agent? The LISP harnesses we found are hard to use unless you already know the language itself, and so we had this idea of simplifying and condensing the UX to be user friendly for the masses, while leveraging the power of LISP. Code as data is what lets an agent change itself, and that shouldn't need a LISP hacker to run. NODECODE is our first step toward putting it on everyone's PC and mobile. You ask in plain words, the model writes LISP, and you get briefed in natural language; that is how it should be.

Extensions? Code as data also suits extensions. We see NODECODE as a living agent organism. To us, it feels very much alive, and so this brings us to the Cells system. A Cell is a folder that teaches NODECODE something new: a chat room it can live in (e.g Discord, Telegram, Slack, etc. - Yes we made Cells for channels to have it act as a very capable personal agent), a skill, a memory, MCPs, new tools, etc. Install one from our Cell hub or ask it to write a custom, personalized one. Either way it is more code the agent can read and change.

Your terminal, a browser tab, your phone and bots in Discord, Telegram and Slack all attach to that SAME gateway process, so a tool it writes in one is there in ALL of them. Over time it becomes yours and it is continuously evolving; the organism within it; NODECODE.

MIT License. https://github.com/nodecode-ai/nodecode X/twitter/demo launch post: https://x.com/pomterree/status/2113721985167728757 docs: https://nodecode.ai/docs

The idea is that you get a call history and you can label calls and later search or browse them to find numbers.

Contact lists are bloated and made for a different time. These days just some plain labels on numbers should be enough.

This approach doesn't discriminate between contacts that are worth adding to a canonical "list of contacts" and people or institutions that have called you only once: everybody can get a label the same way.

I've wanted an app like this to exist for a long time, but never found it, so now I can finally be happy with my sporadic use of the phone dialer again.

story_text.value:
At Researchly (https://www.researchly.at) we automate market and competitive analysis. We learned that on-the-fly web search through AI agents isn't reliable enough for consistent, in-depth work.

Existing data providers such as PitchBook or Crunchbase are either too expensive or lack the data we need: operational signals such as management changes or new partnerships, for DACH. Furthermore, search tools such as Exa tend to be probabilistic. What they return depends on the model and on SEO rankings, so two runs of the same query can give you two different answers.

So we built our own search layer: several providers (Exa, Linkup, Tavily, Parallel), allow/deny lists, source rankings (we once caught ourselves citing our own blog posts), and checks whether an empty result means "nothing there" or "out of budget".

It works, but: it's slow, expensive, non-deterministic & we kept redoing the same research for different clients (which makes it very un-economic).

So we started building the data layer itself. Step one was Firmendaten (300k companies from the Austrian register; shared here last week https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50142669).

Relational data like that is already a huge improvement, but what we really need is a graph, as people ask "W" questions: who does what with whom where and when. This is our first attempt at it.

For now, it just connects who partners with whom and company groups. (Tick "Beziehungen 2. Ebene" to see every partner and person)

It's small (a few dozen robotics companies) but you can already see how complex the graph gets & it serves as a good PoC for us.

We had wanted to build this for a long time, and it turned out to be far harder than we expected. One thing that sounds trivial but was particularly hard: finding the right website for a company.

You can buy that data. There are enrichment APIs that return a company's website. But even if they cover Austrian companies, how do you know which company they matched? There is no worldwide unique company identifier.

And if you do it yourself: how do you know that this website really belongs to this company? You have to validate every single match (e. g. through the imprint on a company's website in Austria).

There are quite a few more challenges involved, but we're happy with where this first, admittedly small, result has landed. Feedback very welcome – especially on which relationships would make a graph like this useful for you.

Feedback welcome!

Hey HN, I wanted to show you something I built. I actually built it last year but the prices of VPS instances went to the moon and I shelved it until recently. It's called Whitehirst (I had the .com domain lying around, hence the name!)

You can spin up a Sovereign UK/EU Windows Workstation in ~10 minutes that's fully configured with all the dev tools you'll need like Visual Studio 2026, VS Code, Docker CE, Git, Rust, NVM, Tailscale and more. It's a custom Windows Server 2022 rig that removes all the bloat, telemetry and Copilot stuff. I've spent an obscene length of time perfecting the build so it runs incredibly fast.

You can spin up a rig for 8 or 24 hours with zero risk of a surprise cloud bill as every workstation is strictly ephemeral and automatically self-destructs when time's up (prices are £12 for 8 hours or £25 for 24 hours). You can extend your time if you wish. I'm only offering a single spec at the moment: 8 AMD EPYC vCPUs, 32GB ECC RAM, 200GB NVMe storage and a 2Gbps nic - I intend to offer other specs later on.

If you'd like to try it, head to https://whitehirst.com and fill out the contact form and I'll pick a handful to get started with. I'm going to keep the numbers small for now so that I can make sure it all works and I can iron out the bugs since it's still in early-access.

Anyway, let me know what you think.

Ta

Mick

story_text.value:
Hey HN, I've been building Sectr, a backend-as-a-service for making it easy(ier) to develop and deploy AI agents. Deploying agents requires non-trivial systems design work. Consider a support agent: how do you stream messages to your frontend, how/where do you persist messages for frontend fetching later (or for auditing), and when the agent wants to issue a refund, do you spin-down the compute infra while it's waiting on human approval? Sectr aims to be the serverless abstraction and platform to provide these systems for you.

No sign-up needed to try using the dev server:

  curl -fsSL https://sectr.dev/install.sh | sh # Install CLI
  sectr init my-agent && cd my-agent # Starter code
  sectr dev # Dev server, with UI to test chatting
Sectr provides:

- Streaming of every token, tool call and event, and persistence so they can be loaded fresh later.

- Scaling up, and down to zero when the agent needs to wait, and resumption right to the suspended agent's state.

- Human approved tools automatically use Sectr's suspension and resumption capabilities, no code needed from you.

- AG-UI endpoint for any deployed agent so you can trivially hook up your frontend

- Local dev server experience, so you can rapidly debug and iterate on your agent's behavior

At the core, you can deploy any container image to Sectr as long as it implements a certain shaped HTTP endpoint. In practice, currently Sectr provides adapters to let you deploy your existing OpenAI Agents SDK, LangGraph, or Pydantic AI agents, with only 2 new lines of code:

  app = AgentApp(name="support")
  app.add_route("/chat", openai_agents(agent))
Certainly the hardest part of building Sectr was getting the resumption logic to be correct and invisible, across the Program State x Model Provider x Agent Framework matrix. For example, an earlier bug was when a model replied with text plus a tool call, Sectr would resume that as two separate messages, instead of one message with a text and tool part. This works, but breaks prompt caching (and might subtly change model behavior).

Sectr is free during the beta (and can be tried locally without sign-up); I mainly want feedback, especially on dev & deployment experiences, any bugs, and what features would excite you.

Introductory video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=H-y3wynkKc0

Docs: https://docs.sectr.dev

story_text.value:
Hi HN, I’m Rayhan. Crulon is a business phone system where an AI agent answers the line and your team works alongside it. You can talk with our demo agent right in your browser, no sign-up: https://crulon.ai/#talk

Why I built it: I’ve spent eight years as a software and network engineer, mostly building tools for internet providers, and kept watching small support teams lose customers in the seams. Calls missed after hours. Calls passed from a bot to a person who had to start over. Most voice AI products are a bot sitting on someone else’s phone line, so a handoff means forwarding to another number and losing the context. We built the phone system and the agent as one thing.

What that gets you:

The handoff happens inside the same system. When something isn’t the AI’s job, it asks the caller, then rings your team (in the browser or on a desk phone) with a note on why they’re calling. Live calls: anyone with permission can listen to an AI call (no one on the call can hear them) and take it over. It’s the same call, with no transfer and no hold music; the AI just leaves. Tools: the agent can call any API you define in an Action builder (look up the caller, open a ticket), and it checks with the caller before changing anything. Outbound campaigns: the agent works through a call list for reminders, renewals and follow-ups, and puts interested people through to your team. SIP desk phones, and bring-your-own-carrier so you can keep your numbers. If you run out of AI minutes, calls follow your fallback route (ring the team, voicemail) instead of dropping, and the refused call isn’t billed.

How it’s built, briefly: calls come in over SIP into Call Flows (menus, queues, schedules), and your team answers in the browser or on SIP desk phones. Each agent runs on one of two engines. Classic transcribes, thinks, then speaks, so you get exact wording and English, Spanish and French. Live is a full-duplex speech model that listens while it talks and hands tool work to a second model. One fun problem with that split was teaching the agent when to hang up, which I wrote up here: https://crulon.ai/blog/teaching-a-voice-agent-to-hang-up

It isn’t a CRM; it works alongside yours. Built-in Apps connect it to systems like billing and network tools, and anything with a web API plugs in through the Action builder.

Pricing is per seat ($24, $49 or $89 a month) with a pool of AI minutes; human calls are included. If you sign up this month, HN30 takes 30% off the first 3 months.

I’ll be here all day. Try the agent, try to trip it up, and tell me what you’d want from a phone system like this.
